newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Heroin traffickers target Vietnam's children.
newsitem.headline: Heroin traffickers target Vietnam's children.

text.p: International heroin traffickers are targetting Vietnam's children in a bid to create a new market in one of East Asia's poorest but most densely populated contries, a U.N. drugs expert said on Thursday.

Joern Kristensen of the United Nations Drugs Control Programme (UNDCP) told Reuters on Thursday that high-grade heroin was appearing in schools across the country, but increasingly in provinces close to the Chinese border as well as in major cities.
"It looks like someone's trying to establish a market," he said. "I think there's no doubt it is organised in one way or another."
According to police reports highest-purity number four grade heroin is being plied to students by food hawkers and others, often immediately outside school and college gates.
Typically it is mixed in cakes and drinks or sold in tiny paper 20 milligram packages.
Kristensen said prices per package ranged from 30,000 dong ($2.70) in the north to 50,000 dong in southern Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City.
"It's being used to chase the dragon. It's not injected. They're just using it to inhale," he said.
Chasing the dragon is a term to describe a method of inhalation typically involving the use of foil over a naked flame.
Vietnam has produced its own opium for many years and continues to do so in some areas despite official attempts to stamp the practice out.

But drugs experts say the communist country is increasingly being used as both a market and conduit for narcotics heading to Australia and the United States from East Asia's notorious Golden Triangle producing area.
According to U.N. information, heroin, cannabis, psychotropic substances and opium are being trafficked in growing quantities in many areas of Vietnam.
Liquid opium, known as "black water", is widely used among drug addicts in Ho Chi Minh City where it sells for around 3,000-5,000 dong (27-45 cents) an injection.
Officials say abuse rates are increasing fast. In the first eight months of this year more heroin was seized than in the whole of 1995.
At the same time drug offences increased by 13 percent over the same period a year earlier, with 70 percent of those arrested below 30 years in age.

Kristensen applauded government moves to tackle the problem and said the United Nations would be announcing a $780,000 training programme in the next few weeks to help Vietnam's law enforcement authorities deal with the matter more effectively.
"We don't know if all the figures are true," he said. "But in one case they took samples at a school and found a third of children had heroin in their urine."
Vietnam is one of the world's poorest countries with per capita income of around $220 a year. But its 75 million people gives it a high population density of 223 persons per square kilometre.
